title: Metabolism – Respiratory chain
blurb: Catabolism vs anabolism; how cells get energy by stepwise oxidation; oxidation and reduction (electron transfer, hydrogenation and dehydrogenation, C–H bonds).
lede: Catabolism vs anabolism; how cells get energy by stepwise oxidation; oxidation and reduction (electron transfer, hydrogenation and dehydrogenation, C–H bonds). Activated carriers (ATP, NADH, NADPH): ATP coupling and condensation reactions (glutamine synthesis), and NAD⁺ vs NADP⁺. Glycolysis (glucose → 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH), then fermentation (lactate, or ethanol + CO₂) vs respiration. The four steps of respiration: glycolysis → citric acid cycle (3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂ per turn) → electron-transport chain (Complex I, ubiquinone, cytochrome b-c1, cytochrome c, cytochrome c oxidase; O₂ → H₂O) → oxidative phosphorylation (~30 ATP per glucose vs 2 from glycolysis). Proteins and fats feed into the same pathways.
six: Oxidation = loss of electrons / dehydrogenation; always paired with reduction
Activated carriers: ATP, NADH, NADPH; NADH (catabolism) vs NADPH (anabolism)

cards.lede: Read the question, answer it out loud, then flip the card.

items.n: Catabolism vs anabolism?
items.a: Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simple ones and releases energy; anabolism uses energy to build molecules.

items.n: How do cells extract energy from food?
Define oxidation in terms of electrons.
Why does oxidation always occur with reduction?
items.a: Electrons are conserved; those removed must be accepted by another molecule.

items.n: Hydrogenation and dehydrogenation correspond to what?
How do C–H bonds change on oxidation?
items.a: Their number decreases (it increases on reduction).

items.n: Name the three main activated carriers.
Is ATP hydrolysis favourable?
items.a: Yes; synthesis from ADP is unfavourable, hydrolysis favourable.

items.n: How does ATP drive a condensation reaction?
items.a: It phosphorylates one molecule into a high-energy intermediate, which then reacts with the second (net: A–B + ADP + Pi + H₂O).

items.n: Which amino-acid synthesis illustrates ATP coupling?
What do NAD⁺/NADP⁺ accept when reduced?
Difference between NAD⁺ and NADP⁺?
items.a: NADP⁺ has an extra phosphate; this changes its shape (different enzymes), not its electron transfer.

items.n: Which carrier serves anabolism and which catabolism?
Where does glycolysis occur, and does it need O₂?
items.a: In the cytosol; no, it is anaerobic.

items.n: What does glycolysis convert, and to what?
Net yield of glycolysis?
items.a: 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose (uses 2, makes 4 ATP).

items.n: What decides fermentation vs respiration?
Why do cells ferment?
items.a: To regenerate NAD⁺ from NADH so glycolysis can continue.

items.n: Products of fermentation?
Which human cells ferment when short of O₂?
Four basic steps of respiration?
items.a: Glycolysis, citric acid cycle, electron-transport chain, oxidative phosphorylation.

items.n: What is pyruvate converted to in the mitochondrion?
Where does the citric acid cycle occur?
First reaction of the citric acid cycle?
Products per turn of the citric acid cycle?
Which step of oxidative catabolism uses O₂ directly?
items.a: Oxidative phosphorylation (the end of the ETC).

items.n: Where are H⁺ pumped by the ETC?
items.a: From the matrix into the intermembrane space.

items.n: What does Complex I contain, and where does it send electrons?
items.a: FMN and 8 Fe–S clusters; to ubiquinone.

items.n: What carries electrons between cytochrome b-c1 and cytochrome c oxidase?
items.a: Cytochrome c (small soluble protein in the crista space, one electron at a time).

items.n: What does cytochrome c oxidase contain?
How many electrons and protons reduce one O₂?
ATP yield of complete glucose oxidation vs glycolysis alone?
Do fats and proteins use the same pathways?
items.a: Yes, they feed into glycolysis, acetyl-CoA and the citric acid cycle.
